What to do now: avoid over-applying nitrogen in the seedbed, as excess nitrogen accelerates blast development. If the infection is spreading rapidly, consult your local extension officer for an approved nursery fungicide and safety instructions. For the next crop cycle, ensure seeds are treated before sowing and select blast-resistant seed varieties.

In fact, low soil moisture and dry rainfed conditions make rice plants much more vulnerable to blast when humidity rises. What you can do: if irrigation water is available, re-establish a shallow flood to reduce plant stress. Avoid applying additional nitrogen fertilizer while the disease is active. If spots continue to expand, seek advice from your local extension worker regarding approved foliar fungicides.

input.user_text: During the branching stage, I found some diamond-shaped spots on the leaves, but I did not worry about them. target_response.user_response: Your crop is suffering from neck blast (panicle blast). The crucial clue is that the whiteheads remain firmly attached when pulled. If stem borers were the cause, the entire white panicle and damaged stem would separate and slide out with zero resistance. What you can do: do not add more nitrogen at this stage. Once neck rot occurs, chemical sprays cannot reverse already blighted heads. Contact your local agricultural extension officer to verify the extent of neck rot, and plan for blast-resistant varieties and balanced fertilizer for next season. Also, I encourage the removal or destruction of all infected plant debris and infected material before next season.
